West Ham United have reportedly joined the race for Stevenage defender Jack Taylor, with the 21-year-old at the moment impressing on loan at Exeter City. However, whilst the Hammers clearly need another centre-back, I’m struggling to understand why we’d be looking at another developing youngster.

Sources indicate that according to Graeme Bailey at TEAMtalk, West Ham are among eight clubs monitoring the 6ft 4in defender, alongside Everton, Brighton, Brentford, Crystal Palace, Fulham, Millwall and Norwich. Taylor recently scored in Exeter’s FA Cup victory over Huddersfield, although there is no confirmation that West Ham had scouts at the match.

It’s clear as day that West Ham need a central defender amongst other positions, but quite why we’d be looking at a 21-year-old from Stevenage is anyone’s guess.

Airidas Golambeckis has represented England at youth level and looks to have incredible potential.

Indeed, his recent performances for England’s Under-20s have strengthened his case for a first-team opportunity, particularly with Max Kilman suspended against Preston.

I’ve been impressed by Golambeckis whenever I’ve seen him, and his performance against Stevenage earlier this year was one of the first occasions when his potential really caught my attention.

Signing Taylor would appear to go against Nils Koppen’s stated recruitment principle of not blocking the pathway of youngsters coming through the academy.

And I think this would definitely be one of those examples.

Airidas Golambeckis has earned the right to play for West Ham.

Don’t get me wrong, I’m not averse to signing an experienced centre-back to see us over the line, in the same way that Axel Disasi came in during January last season.

West Ham’s lack of defensive depth is obvious, and we’ve previously highlighted the need for additional cover during a demanding Championship campaign.

But another young central defender to block the pathway of an exceptional talent at our own club?

And with Claret & Hugh having received confirmation from a club source that Konstantinos Mavropanos is not for sale in January, this shouldn’t be about finding his replacement.

If West Ham are going to strengthen at centre-back, I’d rather they signed somebody experienced enough to make an immediate difference to our promotion prospects.

Taylor might become an excellent defender, but we’ve already got a promising youngster who deserves his chance. Personally, I wouldn’t give this transfer rumour too much attention.

Only one of their eight most valuable goalkeepers doesn’t play for a Premier League club.

That is Joan García, the Barcelona keeper, who is at the very top of the list with an estimated value of €80.6 million (approx £67.4m).

CIES Football Observatory explain that they have looked at ‘the goalkeepers worldwide who right now have the highest estimated transfer value according to our statistical model.’ Their model taking also taking into account the age of the goalkeepers and how long left on their contracts, when establishing their valuations.

Sources indicate that they report: ‘Italy’s Gianluigi Donnarumma (€79.9 million) and Belgium’s Senne Lammers (€64.2 million) round off the top three, with a rising value in fourth place : Aston Villa’s Japanese Zion Suzuki (€59.5 million). Paris Saint-Germain’s and Russia’s Matvey Safonov is the second highest-valued goalkeeper outside the English Premier League (€50.8 million), ahead of Jonas Urbig (Bayern Munich, €50.0 million).’.

Interestingly, amongst the seven Premier League goalkeepers that feature in the top eight, they include Newcastle United and Sunderland goalkeepers….

Build this Newcastle United dream but don’t forget the team

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1181 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The future of NUFC is increasingly being discussed in terms of a new Newcastle United stadium, a redeveloped St James’ Park and an ambitious training complex.
  • These are exciting possibilities but the measure of success will remain what happens on the pitch.
  • The finest facilities in the world will offer little comfort if the Newcastle United team playing in them has been allowed to decline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The future of NUFC is increasingly being discussed in terms of a new Newcastle United stadium, a redeveloped St James’ Park and an ambitious training complex.

These are exciting possibilities but the measure of success will remain what happens on the pitch.

The finest facilities in the world will offer little comfort if the Newcastle United team playing in them has been allowed to decline.

Whether we redevelop our extraordinary home, or eventually move to a new Newcastle United stadium, the possibilities are enormous. More supporters through the turnstiles, better facilities, greater income and a ground that reflects the ambitions we hold for this club.

Then there is the proposed training complex at Woolsington, another substantial statement about where Newcastle United want to go.

Sources indicate that there is much to welcome. But amid the drawings, announcements and debate about what we might build, one question must remain central: what sort of Newcastle United team will be playing there?

Because the finest stadium in the world would offer precious little consolation if we were watching Championship football inside it. Or worse.

That is a warning about priorities, not a prediction of relegation.

Sources indicate that the latest published Fan Advisory Board notes confirm that the club has authorised further work to assess the feasibility of both stadium options. They also record an expected planning application for Woolsington in the second quarter of 2027. These are substantial projects with long horizons and the football club must remain competitive throughout the years required to deliver them.

The East Stand offers a useful historical starting point.

Opened in 1973, it represented a significant improvement to St James’ Park. The ground needed investment, and supporters had good reason to welcome modernisation. We should acknowledge that before turning the story into a convenient argument against building anything.

It has been revealed that but the wider redevelopment envisaged at the time did not materialise. The club’s own history records that recession severely damaged its finances and the East Stand became the only completed phase. Later, looks to rebuild the Leazes End were scuppered by relegation in 1978.

Recent findings suggest that it would be too simplistic to claim that building the East Stand caused Newcastle’s decline. Indeed, we reached the FA Cup final in 1974 and the League Cup final in 1976, before relegation in 1978 and a six-year wait for promotion in 1984. The sequence was more complicated than a new stand followed immediately by a bad team.

The lesson is that an improved ground provides no protection against deteriorating football fortunes. And when those fortunes deteriorate, the assumptions underpinning the grand plans can unravel with them.

That relationship matters today.

Recent findings suggest that A stadium project might be planned over a decade. A team can lose its direction in a season. Recruitment mistakes accumulate, vital players leave, injuries expose weaknesses and confidence drains away. Meanwhile, those responsible for the bigger vision may still be talking confidently about where the club will stand in five years.

Supporters have to live through the intervening Saturdays (or whenever the match might be played these days…).

Photo by Jamie Smith via The Mag.

It has been revealed that none of this means Newcastle should abandon infrastructure investment. A club cannot indefinitely pursue elite ambitions with facilities that constrain its development. More capacity could allow supporters at the moment shut out to attend. Better accessibility matters. Stronger commercial income could help sustain a stronger squad.

The training ground deserves particular recognition because its purpose is directly connected to football performance. The proposed £190 million scheme includes facilities for the men’s first team and academy. Done properly, that investment should improve the environment in which players prepare and young talent develops. There is a convincing case for building.

There must be an equally convincing strategy for the Newcastle United team while the building takes place.

Sources indicate that nor should we pretend that cancelling a construction project would automatically release an identical sum for transfers. Financing arrangements and football spending rules make the relationship more complicated than that. But acknowledging the complexity does not remove the board’s responsibility to explain how its ambitions fit together.

Supporters deserve confidence that the squad’s needs have been properly planned for, that recruitment has clear leadership, and that the club can respond when football takes an unwelcome turn.

Sources indicate that they should also expect the people approving these projects to test uncomfortable possibilities. What happens if construction costs rise? If completion is delayed? If European income fails to arrive? If results fall substantially below expectations?

A credible long-term proposal must be able to withstand something less than the best possible outcome.

In a recent development, there is a Newcastle United example of getting the relationship right, too. In the 1990s, the redevelopment of St James’ Park accompanied an extraordinary revival on the pitch under Kevin Keegan and Sir John Hall. The ground changed as the team gave supporters fresh reasons to believe. Physical development and football ambition advanced together.

That is the standard we should demand now.

Those running the club also need to understand what supporters mean when we talk about ambition. We can appreciate increased revenue, improved hospitality and an impressive training campus. We understand that a successful modern club needs a serious business behind it.

But our most powerful memories are of football.

A goal that sends you into the arms of someone you have never met. A player who lifts an entire crowd when he gets the ball. A team that finds another gear because the ground refuses to let it give up. Taking your child to a match and knowing that, whatever else happens, the two of you will remember it.

Those are the experiences that give a stadium its meaning.

Sources indicate that st James’ Park’s hold on us comes from generations of them. Any redevelopment must respect that connection. Any fresh ground would have to earn it.

According to recent reports, the temptation with enormous projects is that progress becomes easy to display. There are designs to unveil, milestones to announce and buildings to photograph. Building a consistently successful football team is less orderly. It requires judgement, patience, excellent recruitment and the willingness to correct mistakes.

Yet that difficult work remains the central responsibility.

Recent findings suggest that newcastle United should think big. More supporters should have the chance to watch us. Our players and academy prospects should have outstanding facilities. The club should build something that serves the next generation as well as this one.

But those making the decisions must remember how rapidly football can humble a club convinced that its future is assured.

Our history gives us ample reason to keep that thought close.

Recent findings suggest that so pursue the stadium plans. Develop the training ground. Make the investment worthy of Newcastle United and the people who sustain it.

But protect the football throughout.

Let’s build a home for a great Newcastle United team and make sure we keep building the team that deserves to play in it.

  • “The decision by Newham Council represents a significant milestone in the Stadium’s ambition to attract more world-class entertainment and sporting events to East London, delivering increased opportunities for visitors, businesses and the local community.”.
  • The permission will allow London Stadium to increase its annual allocation of concerts and other non-sporting leisure events from 10 to 24, alongside the ability to host up to eight events each year at a maximum capacity of 85,000.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Earlier this week, Newham Council resolved to grant planning permission for changes that will enable the London Stadium to host more major concerts and entertainment events.

London Stadium released a statement saying:.

“The decision by Newham Council represents a significant milestone in the Stadium’s ambition to attract more world-class entertainment and sporting events to East London, delivering increased opportunities for visitors, businesses and the local community.”.

The permission will allow London Stadium to increase its annual allocation of concerts and other non-sporting leisure events from 10 to 24, alongside the ability to host up to eight events each year at a maximum capacity of 85,000.

Sources indicate that there will be no changes to West Ham United’s fixtures or the club’s current matchday capacity of 62,500. No physical changes to the stadium are required.

The application was supported by an economic impact assessment forecasting the potential to generate an additional £15 million for the Newham economy through up to 800,000 additional visits to the stadium each year.

Newly introduced London Stadium CEO Darren Raczkowski remarked:.

According to recent reports, “This is a hugely positive outcome for London Stadium and for East London. We are delighted that Newham Council has recognised the opportunity these changes present, both for the Stadium and the wider local economy.”.

However, on closer scrutiny, you have to ask what the point of increasing to 24 days is and whether the claimed benefits will ever be realised.

Before planning permission was granted, the London Stadium could host up to 10 days of concerts each year, a limit it has never reached in the ten years since opening.

To date, since 2016, no more than five days (half the previous planning permission allowance for concerts) have been used in any single year, so the change seems a bit of wishful thinking to go over ten and reach the dizzy heights of 24 days.

The cost of hosting concerts outside the summer break, while the seats are moved, is likely to be prohibitive. The cost of moving seats remains in the millions, and laying out protective flooring for one concert in an international break could make the venue commercially unattractive, even if the seats remained in place.

The concert venue marketplace is competitive, with Wembley, the O2, Spurs Stadium and Emirates. Brentford are also looking to use their Gtech Community Stadium for future concerts.

Parker Tells West Ham Players An Uncomfortable Championship Truth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that west Ham United manager Scott Parker has identified defensive positioning, transitions and set pieces as areas he intends to improve following the international break.
  • West Ham are the Championship’s highest scorers, but their defensive record has repeatedly undermined their attacking performances.
  • Personally, I’ve always thought there were some relatively easy wins for Parker in terms of fixing West Ham’s defensive problems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that west Ham United manager Scott Parker has identified defensive positioning, transitions and set pieces as areas he intends to improve following the international break. Speaking to talkSPORT this morning, the Hammers boss explained why his team must become more disciplined without sacrificing their attacking ambition.

West Ham are the Championship’s highest scorers, but their defensive record has repeatedly undermined their attacking performances. Parker acknowledged that committing players forward can leave his side exposed, particularly when possession changes hands, and stressed the importance of what his players do behind the ball.

Personally, I’ve always thought there were some relatively easy wins for Parker in terms of fixing West Ham’s defensive problems. We’re scoring plenty of goals; we just need to sort the defence out. And if there’s one thing Parker has demonstrated during his managerial career, it’s that he knows how to organise a team defensively.

During his time at Burnley, Parker oversaw one of the most remarkable defensive campaigns in English football history.

His side conceded just 16 goals across 46 Championship matches during the 2024/25 season, setting a new record and keeping 30 clean sheets on their way to promotion.

Speaking in his talkSPORT interview, Parker discussed the importance of positioning when West Ham commit players forward, explaining that transitions and set pieces are particularly dangerous in the Championship.

And it’s interesting to hear him targeting transitions because that was exactly how West Ham conceded the opening goal against Blackburn Rovers in our last game.

Parker has informed West Ham players that they are now Championship players whether they like it or not.

But perhaps the most interesting part of Parker’s interview was his frank assessment of the mentality required from players who have dropped out of the Premier League.

He pointed out that the demands of the Championship are completely different, with players needing to accept the physical and psychological challenges of the division.

Parker then delivered a particularly pointed observation.

“If there’s a player here at this present moment in time playing in this division, it’s because that’s where he is.”.

It was a way of saying that irrespective of where you come from, it’s where you are that counts.

And no doubt there are players in the West Ham squad who consider themselves to be Premier League, European or international quality.

However, as of right now, they are Championship players, and Parker is quite right to point that out.

The newly introduced gaffer has been promoted from this division three times, so I suspect he knows rather more about what is required than some of the players who have spent most of their careers in the Premier League.

Of course, the international break has given Parker a welcome opportunity to work with his players, although it’s important to remember that ten were away representing their countries.

Nevertheless, he will have learned considerably more about those who remained at Rush Green.

In particular, players such as full-backs Ezra Mayers and Joël Veltman have had the opportunity to work with the new manager, while a good number of West Ham’s midfielders have also remained at the club.

That should have allowed Parker to concentrate on some of the defensive positioning and tactical habits he discussed during the interview.

And let’s not forget that he’ll also have Thursday and Friday’s training sessions to work with his returning internationals ahead of Preston.

That is considerably more preparation time than he enjoyed before his opening two matches against Cardiff and Blackburn.

With four rounds remaining in the Brasileirao, Flamengo host Athletico Paranaense on Wednesday night, November 18, as their title defence enters its decisive stage.

Industry observers note that having collected 92% of the available points in the second half of the season, Flamengo can take a significant step towards back-to-back titles and put themselves in a stronger position ahead of their huge clash against Palmeiras in the following round. Athletico Paranaense, meanwhile, face an uphill task to break back into the top four, having gone four matches without a win and with the tournament's leading scorer unavailable.

In the fight for back-to-back titles and a ninth Brasileirao crown, Flamengo return from this FIFA international break with good news: their key players delivered excellent performances and, more importantly, came back from international duty without any injuries.

According to recent reports, giorgian de Arrascaeta once again took centre stage for the Rubro-Negro with the Uruguay national team. Having had a direct hand in both of Uruguay’s goals against Argentina at the Bombonera, Flamengo’s number 10 also became the first foreigner to have a bust unveiled at the club’s headquarters, in a ceremony on Sunday, November 15.

Industry observers note that bruno Henrique also received the honour and looked ahead to the business end of the season: “We know there is not much left before the year ends, there are four games, so we will give everything in these games to win the title. God willing, we can celebrate in December as well,” he said at the event.

Right-back Guillermo Varela, meanwhile, produced a solid display, playing the full 95 minutes of the match in Buenos Aires. Although Argentina’s goal came down his side, he was not at fault.

Nicolas de la Cruz and Ecuadorians Gonzalo Plata and Anthony Valencia did not leave the bench, but the latter two still have a friendly against Bolivia on Tuesday night, November 17.

Athletico Paranaense, for their part, are enjoying a notable campaign for a newly promoted side. However, in the fight for a direct spot in next season’s Libertadores, the Furacao suffered a heavy blow at Brazil’s sports court (STJD).

In a hearing on Monday, November 16, Kevin Viveros had his ban extended to three matches. The Brasileirão’s top scorer with 21 goals was sent off in the 3-1 defeat to Vasco on November 4, for a stamp on full-back Cuiabano.

Industry observers note that as a result, he will not return until the final round, against Sao Paulo at the Arena da Baixada. Jorge Rivaldo and Renan Peixoto are the natural options given their profile, but manager Odair Hellmann could also opt to use forward Kerwin Vargas in an adapted role.

Recent findings suggest that in the same hearing, the Parana side were also punished. The fine for racist gestures attributed to a fan during the match against Vasco was increased to R$30,000 (approximately £4,200). The decision was taken by a majority of votes.

Sources indicate that currently fifth with 54 points, Athletico could close the gap on Fluminense, who occupy the final Libertadores spot. Bahia and Atletico Mineiro, however, are also in the same points range.

Athletico Paranaense Brasileiro form:.

In a late development, Gonzalo Plata was released from the Ecuador squad for “personal reasons” and could become an unexpected boost. Having played just 13 minutes against Costa Rica, he should not, in theory, show any physical wear.

Nicolas de la Cruz and Anthony Valencia remain with their national teams and are not expected to return in time.

On the medical front, experienced left-back Alex Sandro has recovered from muscular oedema in his left thigh and has returned to training with the group, although Ayrton Lucas is expected to be the first choice for Portuguese manager Leonardo Jardim.

Industry observers note that midfielder Lucas Paqueta has not yet fully recovered from a knee problem sustained during the thrashing of Vasco, so he is unlikely to be included without a reasonable amount of training, according to Jardim himself. Danilo, meanwhile, continues his recovery schedule following a jaw fracture and also remains sidelined.

The point of concern is the number of players one booking away from suspension: Leo Pereira, Alex Sandro, Erick Pulgar, Arrascaeta, Pedro, Bruno Henrique, Luiz Araujo and Vitao. Should any of them be booked by referee Rafael Klein, they would miss the clash against Palmeiras in the following round.

In a recent development, besides Viveros, Dantas is also serving a suspension due to the automatic one-match ban for a third yellow card. Young centre-back Arthur Dias, who is attracting interest from several European clubs, is another absentee. He is set to play for the Brazil national team against Singapore and is not expected to return to Brazil in time.

Defender Lucas Esquivel is still recovering from a hip injury and will be assessed on matchday, but he is expected to complete the back line alongside Gaston Benavidez and Juan Aguirre. Goalkeeper Santos and Bruno Zapelli could be given a chance in the starting eleven.

Flamengo possible starting lineup:.

Industry observers note that agustin Rossi; Varela, Leo Pereira, Leo Ortiz, Ayrton Lucas; Pulgar, Jorginho, Arrascaeta; Carrascal, Pedro, Samuel Lino. Manager: Leonardo Jardim.

Athletico Paranaense possible starting lineup:.

Santos; Benavidez, Aguirre, Esquivel; Gilberto, Luiz Gustavo, Jadson, Mendoza; Bruno Zapelli, Joao Cruz, Kerwin Vargas. Manager: Odair Hellmann.

Athletico's task would have been difficult enough as it is, but with their top scorer and best defender both unavailable, it is hard to see the visitors taking anything from this encounter.

According to recent reports, for Flamengo, the priority will be to maintain their formidable home record and head into the most eagerly anticipated game of the year in a favourable position. A convincing victory at the Maracana would be the ideal way to achieve that.

Recent findings suggest that if this is Tuchel-ball, if this is the way Thomas Tuchel wants England to play, then yes, please. More of the same; bring it on. The standard is set.

According to recent reports, england’s DNA? This was a total-football annihilation of a top nation. Croatia, 14th in the world and fierce competitors, were cowed and humiliated at home in this Nations League tie. This was the biggest defeat in their proud history – seventh heaven for England, and hell for the hosts.

The visitors were sublime. Harry Kane (twice – 89 goals now for his country), Jude Bellingham and Anthony Gordon all scored and were outstanding. Bukayo Saka also struck twice. Alex Scott made his first start and will take some dislodging. The Bournemouth midfielder was slick with a snap – perpetual, intelligent, smooth motion.

It has been revealed that harry Kane at the DOUBLE! 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿The Three Lions have FIVE in Rijeka 🦁 pic.twitter.com/BRnVXADtHC.

Sources indicate that but here the standard was set – it was an exhilarating example of the football England are capable of. On display we saw the speed, the movement, the passes under pressure, the ambition, the control and aggression. This was the full package. Bottle it. Bag it. Believe it.

Sources indicate that croatia have an ageing team and are in transition, but they were left looking callow. It looked as though it was men against boys. There were plenty of boys in the stands, with 6,200 children allowed in for what was supposed to be a behind-closed-doors fixture – Croatia’s punishment for crowd trouble.

Their fresh head coach Slaven Bilic would doubtless have been relieved that the match was not played in front of the usual, passionate, partisan crowd. Even then some of the kids booed and left early. Bilic looked shell-shocked. As well he might.

Kane’s commitment was incredible. At one stage Croatia substitute Kristijan Jakić threatened to break clear but was stopped by England’s last man tracking back. It was Kane, one cap short of equalling Peter Shilton’s all-time record of 125 appearances, and it was already 5-0 when that happened.

Sources indicate that these could be exciting times for England. Times when they have shaken off the debate over how well or otherwise they did at the World Cup and moved on. Tuchel has talked up that third-place finish; we have tended to dwell on the semi-final exit to Argentina.

And now? If Tuchel does go and win a trophy for England, he will be talking about this game. Previously he referenced the 5-0 demolition of Serbia in Belgrade, during the World Cup qualification. But the Serbians were a rabble. Croatia are not, but were made to look so on Saturday.

Where will this sit among England performances? There was the 2-1 victory away to Italy at the beginning of the Euro 2024 qualification campaign in March 2023. Before that, the 3-2 win away to Spain in 2018, also in the Nations League. But England were more thrilling here. Do we have to go back to 5-1 in Munich in 2001?

Recent findings suggest that the concern will be the familiar England problem of looking like world-beaters in the autumn and worn out by the time a tournament comes around in the summer. But against Croatia there was control and authority as they raised their chances of finishing in the top two and qualifying for next March’s quarter-finals.

Recent findings suggest that the goals rained in – even if the best remained the first as Marc Guéhi intercepted a clearance, Scott took the ball on the half-turn and found Bellingham. He slid it through to Kane who finished high into the net. What a goal.

Even before half-time England were not finished as Bellingham crossed low from the left and found Saka, who found the back of the net.

According to recent reports, after the break, the hunger remained insatiable. Anderson was sent down the right and Kane slid in. Croatia then lost the ball sloppily inside their own area, Kane thought about shooting but unselfishly fed Saka, who claimed a second goal.

Saka should have had a hat-trick before substitute Morgan Rogers wrapped up the scoring, collecting a ball over the top from the relentless Bellingham – once again captain after Kane went off – and finishing with ease after rounding the goalkeeper. Thomas Tuchel was glowing about Alex Scott in his pre-match media duties ahead of today’s game against Croatia and the midfielder has been handed his first England start.

Scott has come in for Myles Lewis-Skelly in what looks to be an attacking change from Tuchel, the England head coach.

Tuchel had taken Scott to the United States on his pre-World Cup training camp, but the Bournemouth midfielder was not part of the squad for the tournament-proper.

According to recent reports, on Scott, Tuchel stated: “I am super impressed by Alex Scott, I think he is at the moment one of the best central midfielders in the Premier League and he just proves it in every training session. He had a fantastic debut the other day and really really impressed me.”.

Jordan Pickford has revealed he spends up to three hours talking to a “mindwork coach”.

The England goalkeeper has worked with sports psychologists for some time but has gone into detail about how committed he is as he faces a challenge to his No 1 spot from James Trafford.

Pickford will start for England in the Nations League tie against Croatia, and next Tuesday’s fixture at home to the Czech Republic, having missed out on the past two games.

Trafford was in goal for the 3-2 loss to Spain and the 2-0 victory away to the Czechs and although Thomas Tuchel has remarked Pickford remains his first choice it is known that he and his coaching staff are huge admirers of Leeds United’s upcoming goalkeeper.

Trent Alexander-Arnold is expected to drop back down to the substitutes’ bench for England’s third Nations League game against Croatia in Rijeka.

Despite Alexander-Arnold providing an assist for Anthony Gordon against the Czech Republic, England head coach Thomas Tuchel is expected to replace him with Jarell Quansah at right-back.

According to recent reports, jude Bellingham is also in line for a recall, most likely in place of Morgan Rogers, while Tuchel had been hopeful of Ezri Konsa returning to fitness to replace Trevoh Chalobah in the centre of defence. Goalkeeper Jordan Pickford replaces James Trafford.

Uefa fined the Croatian football federation £80,000 and ordered them to play their next Uefa-sanctioned home match behind closed doors because of their fans’ racist chanting and for fireworks offences during a Nations League match against France in 2025. Croatia have played Fifa-sanctioned World Cup qualifiers and friendlies at home in front of fans since but tonight is the first in Uefa competition and hence the ban.

However, a caveat in Uefa’s disciplinary regulations allows the home federation in such circumstances to fill the ground to 75 per cent of its capacity with “children up to the age of 14 (duly accompanied) from schools and/or football academies invited to the match free of charge”. And given the scrum outside the stadium this afternoon, that is what is happening.

Good afternoon and welcome to live coverage of England’s Uefa Nations League Group A3 match against Croatia in Rijeka. Matches between the two are relatively frequent – 12 in 30 years. Croatia have beaten England three times in the 10 competitive meetings, home and away in qualification for Euro 2008, which dealt the England manager a blow from which he could not recover, and the World Cup semi-final in Moscow in 2018.

The extraordinary thing about both the first two defeats – the ‘Wally with the Brolly’ match in November 2007, Steve McLaren’s last in charge, and the home tie on October 10 2006 – is that Luka Modric played in both. And now eight days shy of 20 years since his first appearance against England, he is still running their midfield at the age of 41.

England have had the upper hand since Russia, winning in the Nations League at Wembley in 2018, opening their Euro 2020 campaign with a 1-0 victory by virtue of Raheem Sterling’s goal and then in June when they were at their fluent best, a rare occurrence, in the second half of their first World Cup group game to push on from 2-2 to finish 4-2.

Slaven Bilic, manager from 2006-12, is back in charge for his second spell but his squad still relies heavily on experienced players. Modric is the eldest but is joined by greybeard stalwarts Ivan Perisic, Ante Budimir and Andrej Kramaric, both 35. Spain hammered them 4-1 in midweek after they had started with a 2-1 victory over Czech Republic in Prague.

England, who rattled Spain and should have gone 3-1 up but lost 3-2, were much better in the second half in Prague against a team reduced to 10 men and deserved their 2-0 win, have played at the tiny Stadion Rujevica (capacity 8,279) once before, drawing 0-0 in 2018.

Industry observers note that thomas Tuchel, who changed three of his back four on Tuesday, may stick with Lewis Hall after he made a positive impression in combination with Anthony Gordon. As for Trent Alexander-Arnold, who set up the first goal, Tuchel does not go out of his way to undermine the perception that for all his unique quality, he just doesn’t fancy the Real Madrid right-back at all.

It’s up to Alexander-Arnold to make a compelling case if picked today or at Wembley on Tuesday to persuade the German head coach not to restore his beloved if brittle ‘Reecey’ James at the first opportunity.

It has been revealed that calciomercato.com write that the Rossoneri are beginning to take an interest in Nathan Ngoy, the Belgian defender who is rapidly progressing. Like Diego Moreira, he also scored his first goal for the Red Devils against Italy and the future looks bright for him.

Remarked to be following in Vincent Kompany’s footsteps, he’s part of the rebuilding of the Belgian defence and has become a starter since the World Cup.

It’s also a reason why his value has risen so much in recent months; after the summer, he was believed to be worth €20 and €25 million, but he’s now got a valuation of around €40m.

Goncalo Inacio and Virgil van Dijk are the main names for the defence right now. Yet, the links between the Diavolo and Lille could help make a route to Ngoy easier, as could his international teammates who play at San Siro.

Newcastle and Aston Villa are also keen on the young defender, so he’s certainly one to watch in the future and it could be a major coup for Milan.
